extracted.intended_audience: news editors, newsroom managers, journalism researchers, media policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: A standardized content-analysis / coding scheme and related evaluative criteria for classifying news stories (soft vs hard), story frames, tone, and other attributes used to study news content and its civic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft news vs. Hard news (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard news: coverage of breaking events involving top leaders, major issues, or significant disruptions in routines of daily life (e.g., earthquake, airline disaster) that is important to citizens' ability to understand and respond to public affairs. Soft news: news that has no clear connection to public policy; by this residual standard, all news not of the above type is 'soft.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soft news can also be defined by characteristics (sensational, personality-centered, less time‑bound, practical, incident‑based) or vocabulary (greater SELF‑REFERENCE, lower COLLECTIVES/COMPLEXITY). The report measures proportion of stories without a public policy component to operationalize soft news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of Soft News
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes commonly used to identify soft news: more sensational, more personality‑centered, less time‑bound, more practical ('news you can use'), and more incident‑based than other news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: increased proportion of human‑interest stories, dramatic incidents (crime/disaster), and 'news you can use' pieces. Use DICTION categories (e.g., HUMAN INTEREST, SELF‑REFERENCE) and content coding frames (human interest, sensationalism, news_you_can_use) to operationalize.

rubrics_metrics.name: DICTION vocabulary metrics (collectives, self‑reference, complexity, human interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dictionary-based textual measures used to detect vocabulary shifts: COLLECTIVES (words reflecting categorical thought/social groupings), SELF‑REFERENCE (first‑person references), COMPLEXITY (average word length measure), HUMAN INTEREST (personal pronouns, family terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decline in COLLECTIVES and COMPLEXITY and increase in SELF‑REFERENCE and HUMAN INTEREST are consistent with softening of news. Use automated DICTION scoring to quantify changes in vocabulary across stories/media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of Story
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorization of the lead (focus) of the story: basically straight/hard news (event or incident within past 24 hours), balanced mix of straight news and analysis, mainly news analysis, feature/human interest, or verbatim text/interview/speech/document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus coding should prioritize the lead. Examples: a factual event lead = straight news; interpretive pieces = analysis; anecdotal pieces = feature/human interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus of Story
rubrics_metrics.description: Key focus of the story: current/ongoing event or development; current incident; update on past event; update on past incident; upcoming event; or non‑event/non‑incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'incident' (small, isolated, personal event, e.g., a crime) from 'event' (broader social implications). The peg (timeliness) may differ from the story's focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salience of Story (why it's in today's news)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scale indicating why the story appears now: from unavoidable/magnitudinous and timely (1) to arbitrary choice/no notable salience (5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use editorial judgment about magnitude and timeliness: e.g., major disaster = highest salience; minor item possibly chosen = lower salience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of Story
rubrics_metrics.description: Origin of the story: news outlet byline, news outlet no byline, news outlet's wire service, compiled from wire services, AP, Reuters/UPI, NYT or other news‑outlet‑based wire, other identified source, or source not identifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies whether story was generated in‑house or from external wire/agency; helps assess agenda origins and potential sourcing bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Location (placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Placement of the story within the medium (page number or order in newscast).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With TV, code relative order (be aware some outlets list stories in reverse order). Placement signals editorial priority (lead story vs late item).

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Length
rubrics_metrics.description: Length of story measured (word count or equivalent), with codes for indeterminate or exceeding coding limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer pieces may indicate more depth/analysis; very short items often signal brief incident coverage or fillers.

rubrics_metrics.name: News Section
rubrics_metrics.description: Section/category in which the story appears (e.g., national, metro, other, indeterminate, television news).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Location within a publication/newscast helps contextualize whether a story is presented as public affairs or feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public / Private Frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the story is framed in the public affairs/public realm (including public actors) or in the private realm (celebrity, private institutions, personal lives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public affairs stories include government actors or public‑realm topics (a crime story may be public if it has public policy implications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy / Non‑Policy Frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which the story has relevance for public policy: substantially policy related, somewhat policy related, or non‑policy related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy relatedness must be stated in the story. A crime report without reference to public safety policy may be coded non‑policy; election polling without policy implications may be non‑policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action / Non‑Action Frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the story implies or states there is an urgent need for action (1), non‑urgent need for action (2), action already taken/being taken (3), or no action component (4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If action is implied, determine urgency and whether action is public or personal. Only code attribution of responsibility if an action frame is coded 1–3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of Responsibility Frame
rubrics_metrics.description: If the story implies action is needed, who is seen as responsible: government/public official(s); a group/collective/community/private institution; or a private individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This code follows Action/Non‑Action; it identifies the locus of responsibility for remedy or change as portrayed in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: News You Can Use
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the story's primary purpose is to offer personal advice or practical information (primary purpose, secondary purpose, not the purpose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical 'news you can use' items include health, consumer, or safety advice targeted at individuals rather than public policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual Frame (episodic vs thematic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the story places an event in a narrow episodic/case‑study context or in a broader thematic context that deals with societal meaning, trends, or implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodic stories focus on specific events/individuals; thematic stories analyze trends or systemic implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict / Non‑Conflict Frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of conflict in story presentation: substantial level of conflict, some conflict (not merely incidental), or no/insignificant conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the story is presented—are opposing actors juxtaposed, is there quarrel/blame, or is the story non‑conflictual?

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: If conflict is present, whether it is actual (real, observable conflict between participants) or synthetic (conflict imposed by the reporter through juxtaposed interviews/speculation) or cannot determine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish reporter‑constructed conflict from genuine adversarial exchanges among actors; synthetic conflict can indicate dramatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human‑Interest Frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of human‑interest content: high, moderate, slight, or none. Human interest uses personal examples, human faces on issues, private life detail, or emotive adjectives/vignettes generating sympathy/empathy/outrage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to operationalize soft/news feature content; high human interest often signals personalization rather than policy focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative / Positive Frame (valence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the story is overall clearly negative/unfavorable through neutral to clearly positive/favorable (multi‑point scale from clearly negative to clearly positive/neutral).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: if you were the subject's press secretary, would you consider this favorable? For institutions/developments, is it good or bad for society?

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism Frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a story is hyped or presented breathlessly: high, moderate, low sensationalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tone, adjectives, hyped presentation rather than substance. Sensationalism often correlates with soft news strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Ambiance (tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone of the story irrespective of topic: serious/important; matter‑of‑fact; or lighthearted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiance helps distinguish gravitas: serious ambiance aligns more with hard news; lighthearted with soft features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic Style
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the story is descriptive (telling 'what' happened) or interpretive/analytical/evaluative (explaining, analyzing, evaluating while describing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive style implies analysis and may indicate higher informational depth; descriptive style is straightforward reporting of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft News / Hard News Classification (coder judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A discrete coder classification ranging from 'definitely a soft news story' to 'definitely a hard news story' with intermediate categories (mostly soft, mixed, mostly hard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This integrates multiple frames (policy relevance, human interest, sensationalism, tone, etc.) to assign an overall soft/hard label for each story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic Arena
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic scope of the story: foreign/international (no U.S. component), foreign with significant U.S. component, national (with or without foreign link), regional, state, local, or none/no location context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geographic arena indicates scope and audience relevance; helps compare local vs national tendencies toward softening/critical tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Lead (type of lead)
rubrics_metrics.description: What leads the story: a political/governmental personality, nonpolitical personality, expert person, ordinary/unknown person, institution/agency of government, group/organization, corporation/business entity, or country/state/city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead type signals personalization vs institutional focus; personalities as leads often signal softening or human‑interest orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main Actor / Realm Code
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific coding for principal actors/realms when applicable (e.g., President/White House, Cabinet officer/federal agency, Member of Congress, Supreme Court/federal judiciary, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when story's main actor is a government or political institutional actor to capture which public realm is featured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major Topic Code
rubrics_metrics.description: Topical classification for the story: government & policy, politics (campaign/vote/strategy), political scandal, political personality, business & commerce, celebrity, crime, natural disasters, manmade disasters, science, technology, medicine, personal health, media, entertainment/arts/fashion/travel, food, religion, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to group stories by substantive domain; note when topics cross policy/non‑policy lines (e.g., business vs economic policy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Major Issue Code
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific issue categories for public‑policy stories: economy (inflation, trade, taxes, budgets), health, welfare/poverty, education, public safety, war & peace, terrorism, national defense, foreign affairs, immigration, environment, race/gender issues, crime as broad issue, drugs, criminal justice, technology as policy, communications policy, social security, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides granular issue‑level classification for policy‑relevant stories; use memo sheet to record issues not listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major Context Frame
rubrics_metrics.description: General narrative context of the story: ambition/power frame (winning/losing, strategy), conflict (blame/infighting), cooperation (working together), problem/policy frame (identifying/explaining problems and policy solutions), human interest frame, or none/other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context frame complements episodic/thematic coding and helps identify whether coverage privileges strategy/conflict over policy substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived News Quality Attributes (public perceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience perception dimensions used to evaluate news quality: informative/uninformative; interesting/boring; enjoyable/not enjoyable; depressing/uplifting; negative/positive; superficial/thorough; biased/fair; accurate/misleading; sensational/serious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These attributes were asked in surveys (Figure 8) to gauge how audiences evaluate overall news quality and to relate perceptions to content trends (soft/critical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Preference Measure (hard vs soft)
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey measure asking whether respondents prefer 'news that sticks mainly to stories about major events and issues' (hard news) or 'news that focuses on specific incidents such as a crime or fire or accident' (soft news); follow‑ups ask tolerance for soft/hard news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to segment 'hard news consumers' vs 'soft news consumers' and relate preferences to consumption patterns and demographic attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline Interest Test (indirect preference measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Battery of representative hard and soft news headlines; respondents indicate interest in reading a story with each headline to infer preferences less subject to social desirability bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as an indirect test of content preferences; used to validate direct preference questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Consumption Metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of regular exposure: percent who 'regularly' read daily paper news pages, regularly watch local TV news, regularly watch national cable/broadcast news, regularly listen to radio news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compare consumption levels across hard vs soft news consumers and across media (e.g., NPR audience composition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust / Political Interest Indicators (outcome measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of political trust and interest used to evaluate consequences of critical journalism: trust in government, belief in honesty of government officials, interest in public affairs 'most of the time' vs 'now and then.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are outcome metrics (from NES and other sources) linked to content patterns (rising negativity/critical journalism) to assess civic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative Coverage Tracking (tone over time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Counting/measurement of negative vs positive coverage of political actors (e.g., presidential candidates, Congress, agencies) over time to assess critical journalism trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use longitudinal content counts (e.g., Figure 12) to measure rising negativity and relate to public opinion indicators like trust and interest.
